source: Kenneth Grahame, The Wind in the Willows (1908), Project Gutenberg eBook #289
passages: It was so very beautiful that the Mole could only hold up both forepaws and gasp, "O my! O my! O my!"

As he hurried along, eagerly anticipating the moment when he would be at home again among the things he knew and liked, the Mole saw clearly that he was an animal of tilled field and hedge-row, linked to the ploughed furrow, the frequented pasture, the lane of evening lingerings, the cultivated garden-plot.
"I think it must be the field-mice," replied the Mole, with a touch of pride in his manner.
Here we stand in the cold and the sleet, Blowing fingers and stamping feet, Come from far away you to greet- You by the fire and we in the street- Bidding you joy in the morning!
The Toad retraced his weary way on foot, and related his disappointing experiences to the Water Rat once more.
"Hooray! Here's old Toad!" cried the Mole, his face beaming. "Fancy having you back again!" And he began to dance round him.
The goodnatured Mole picked up a stick, formed his prisoners up in a line on the floor, gave them the order "Quick march!" and led his squad off to the upper floor.
Hence forth I will be a very different Toad. My friends, you shall never have occasion to blush for me again.
